summary.text: When a field K sits inside a larger field L and K uses the operations of L restricted to K, L is called an extension field of K and K a subfield of L.
For example, the complex numbers are an extension field of the real numbers, and the real numbers are a subfield of the complex numbers.
Field extensions are fundamental in algebraic number theory and in the study of polynomial roots through Galois theory, and are widely used in algebraic geometry.

facts.value: The complex numbers extend the real numbers

facts.value: The degree is 1 exactly when the two fields are equal

facts.label: Quadratic and cubic
facts.value: Extensions of degree 2 and 3 have these names

facts.value: A subfield has the same characteristic as the larger field

facts.value: One exists for any polynomial over K, splitting it into linear factors

items.prompt: The complex numbers contain the real numbers and use the same addition and multiplication. How are the two fields related?

options.label: The reals are an extension field of the complex numbers
The complex numbers are an extension field of the reals
Neither contains the other, so they are unrelated
They are the same field written two ways

items.explain: The complex numbers are an extension field of the real numbers, and the real numbers are a subfield of the complex numbers.

items.prompt: An extension has degree 1. What does that tell you about the two fields?

options.label: They are equal, so the extension is trivial
The larger field has exactly one new element
The extension is quadratic
The smaller field has no elements

items.explain: The degree of an extension is 1 if and only if the two fields are equal, which makes it a trivial extension.

items.prompt: A field extension has degree 3. What is it called?

options.label: A quadratic extension
A trivial extension
A finite extension only in characteristic 0
A cubic extension

items.explain: Extensions of degree 2 and 3 are called quadratic and cubic extensions respectively; both are also finite, since their degree is finite.

items.prompt: A smaller field has a certain characteristic, and you move to a larger field that contains it. What can you say about the larger field's characteristic?

options.label: It is the same as the smaller field's
It is always zero
It is always a different prime
It could be anything at all

items.explain: The characteristic of a subfield is the same as the characteristic of the larger field.

items.prompt: You take all ratios of two polynomials with coefficients in a field K, and call the result K(X). What is this field to the polynomial ring K[X]?

options.label: Its subring of constant terms
Its field of fractions
Its splitting field over K
Its quotient by a maximal ideal

items.explain: The elements of K(X) are fractions of two polynomials over K, and K(X) is the field of fractions of the polynomial ring K[X].

items.prompt: You have a polynomial with coefficients in K and want a larger field where it breaks into a product of linear factors. Is that possible?

options.label: No, this only works for degree 2
No, the extension would be a smaller field
Only if K is the real numbers
Yes, by building extensions step by step

items.explain: Iterating the construction yields a splitting field of any polynomial from K[X], an extension field in which the polynomial splits into linear factors.

paragraphs.heading: What a field extension is
paragraphs.text: A field extension is a pair of fields: a smaller one, K, sitting inside a larger one, L, where K adds and multiplies exactly as L does when you stay inside K. We then call L an extension field of K, and K a subfield of L. The shorthand for the pair is L / K, said aloud as "L over K".

paragraphs.heading: Familiar examples
paragraphs.text: The rational numbers sit inside the real numbers, and the real numbers sit inside the complex numbers, so each step is a field extension. Stacking the two steps means C / Q is an extension too. A field caught between the two ends of an extension, as R sits between Q and C, is called an intermediate field.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring size with degree
paragraphs.text: In an extension L / K, the larger field L can be treated as a vector space over K. The dimension of that space is the degree of the extension, written [L : K]. The degree is 1 exactly when the two fields are the same, and that case is called a trivial extension. Degree 2 gives a quadratic extension, degree 3 a cubic one, and any extension of finite degree is called a finite extension.

paragraphs.heading: Adjoining new elements
paragraphs.text: Pick some set S of elements of L. The smallest subfield of L that holds both K and S is written K(S), read "K adjoin S", and S is said to generate it over K. When S is one element s, the extension K(s) / K is called simple and s is called a primitive element. In characteristic 0, every finite extension turns out to be simple; this is the primitive element theorem, and it fails for fields of nonzero characteristic.

paragraphs.heading: Building a missing root
paragraphs.text: A common way to make an extension is to create a root for a polynomial that has none. Suppose K has no element whose square is −1. Then X² + 1 is irreducible in K[X], and the quotient K[X] / (X² + 1) is a larger field that does contain a square root of −1, namely the class of X. Repeating this trick builds a splitting field for any polynomial: a field where it breaks completely into linear factors.

paragraphs.heading: Where extensions matter
paragraphs.text: Finite extensions of Q go by the name algebraic number fields and matter in number theory, as do the p-adic numbers Q_p, an extension of Q that is not finite. For each prime p and positive integer n there is, up to isomorphism, exactly one finite field with pⁿ elements, and it extends the prime field with p elements. More broadly, field extensions are basic tools in algebraic number theory, in Galois theory's study of polynomial roots, and in algebraic geometry.
